name: Daria Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential; please tell me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and an experienced developer at a tech company that runs an ordering platform for a food cooperative. I have a bachelor's degree and spend my day fixing stock records, checking payment batches and explaining late orders to the warehouse team. I'm competent at the work, though I'm not the person who solves every strange fault alone. I like when a delivery driver gets a clear list instead of a rushed apology.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household situation around your job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans offices on shifts, and we have children aged eight and thirteen and a mortgage. My pay is low for an experienced developer, we have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar jobs nearby. I have never used an AI coding tool. I would rather ask a coworker to show me the record than trust a new answer I cannot trace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers a little automatic sorting is fine if warehouse staff can still correct a wrong order. I wouldn't buy a tool just to say we're modern. The cooperative needs a reliable pick list more than a faster slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI hype fading would not make our mortgage easy. A missed cleaning shift can wipe out the little we have saved, and my lower developer pay is already stretched. I still have work, but one bad month would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking stock records with the warehouse lead and maintain our present release routine. Starting this week, we'd stop buying snacks at the station after school and put the freed money into an emergency account when the mortgage is paid. In the first year I'd keep the same checks and ask the staff committee to record any repeated order mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The software is manageable, but the bills aren't generous. I can sound calm at work and still count the days until the mortgage leaves the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which wrong order stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver was sent to collect six crates that were never in the cold room. The food-order screen looked tidy, and the delivery driver lost an hour. I want the warehouse staff able to mark the count wrong before a van leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the snack cut save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 20 each month if we keep it up. I'd rather explain to the children that we bring food from home than ask my partner to make up another shift. It is small, but it is new cash.

say: I'd accept **small sorting tools** only if warehouse staff can correct wrong orders.
I'd put **reliable pick lists** ahead of a faster software claim.
think: I worry our **mortgage** remains fragile even when AI changes little.
My **lower pay** and my partner's uncertain cleaning shifts leave almost no buffer.
do: Keep **checking stock records** with the warehouse lead before releases.
Stop **station snacks** this week and save about 20 monthly after the mortgage is paid.
feel: **Anxious** about existing mortgage pressure despite modest AI change.
S0.quote: The food-order screen looked tidy, and the delivery driver lost an hour.
fieldNote: Her caution comes from a **six-crate mistake** that wasted a driver's time.
A thin buffer and variable **cleaning shifts** explain anxiety even under mild AI change.
The snack cut frees **about 20 monthly** for genuinely new emergency savings.

steps.text: Keep checking cooperative stock records with the warehouse lead
Stop buying after-school snacks at the station this week
Transfer about 20 monthly from the snack cut after the mortgage clears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write stock updates and answer customers, so staff should see the plan before jobs quietly disappear. I'd ask our worker committee to count vacancies the company stops filling and invite warehouse staff to the meeting. Their hours can be cut by a bad screen too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company could keep one developer to check AI output and cut the rest, including me. I know the cooperative's messier orders, but I don't know if that protects my wage. We cannot pay the mortgage on cleaning shifts alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'd attend the worker committee and request written staffing numbers. If management proves its new stock tool catches the missing-crate cases and gives paid supervised time, I'd learn it on fake orders, though I don't want to rush live use. In the first year, if my hours fall, we'd cancel the planned weekend trip and I'd apply for remote inventory-support roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect a big income cut is possible here, and the household has almost no room to wait. I hate being pushed toward a tool before the people who lift the crates have tested it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would warehouse staff ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd ask who signs off a pick list when a crate count is wrong. I'd put that question in the committee's letter. A warehouse worker shouldn't lose a shift because a software mistake is called efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI. Would you really learn this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the missing-crate cases pass and I get paid time beside a colleague who knows the tool. I would ask to see its wrong answers first. I won't pay for private lessons to protect a low wage.

say: I'd ask the **worker committee** to count unfilled jobs and include warehouse staff.
I'd demand **human pick-list checks** before AI changes customer and stock work.
think: I expect a **large wage cut** if the company keeps fewer developers.
My partner's **cleaning shifts** cannot cover our mortgage alone.
do: Attend the **worker committee** next week and request written staffing numbers.
Learn the **new stock tool** only after it passes old crate cases with paid supervision.
Cancel the **weekend trip** and apply for remote inventory support if hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and almost no waiting room in the budget.
S1.quote: A warehouse worker shouldn't lose a shift because a software mistake is called efficiency.
fieldNote: She reaches for **worker representation** before accepting a staffing plan.
Her AI resistance softens only with **proved cases** and **paid supervision**.
Trip cancellation and remote applications depend on **reduced paid hours**.

steps.text: Attend worker committee and request written developer staffing numbers
Learn new stock tool only after old cases pass and paid supervision is offered
Cancel planned weekend trip if developer hours fall
Apply for remote inventory support roles if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff full thinking AI by 2028 could do our coding and orders before robots reach warehouse lifting around 2031. I'd ask the committee for written notice and a way for cooperative members to challenge a wrong delivery. The later robots don't buy my screen job time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer wage could end. We have less than a month saved, my partner's shifts change, and there are few nearby developer jobs. I cannot see a paid route ready in two years. The mortgage does not pause while I find a paid route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tonight I'd bring the mortgage figures to the worker committee and ask them to press for paid transition time. We'd cancel the weekend trip now and ask my sister if she knows of paid warehouse-office openings; I would not assume she can hire me. If laid off in the first year after 2028, I'd apply to a paid cooperative office vacancy only if one exists and the combined wage covers mortgage and food; I'd ask about public training help before paying any fee, but I have no course picked out yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I have calls I can make, but no money or agreed job to bridge a lost wage. I can picture the children at dinner while I try to explain a payment notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your sister actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister works at another warehouse and can tell me when paid office hours open, not promise me a place. I'd ask her for a lead, not rent money. If there is nothing, I still have to look elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the mortgage, food and school costs in one column and our savings in another. I wouldn't tell the children a new job is waiting. We'd agree which bill to protect first.

say: I'd demand **written notice** as 2028 thinking AI reaches our orders and code.
I'd ask for a **member appeal** before software sends wrong deliveries.
think: I expect my **developer wage** to end with almost no savings behind it.
I cannot see a **funded bridge** through a two-year shock and a mortgage.
do: Bring **mortgage figures** to the worker committee and press for paid transition time tonight.
Cancel the **weekend trip** and ask my sister about paid office leads without assuming a vacancy.
Apply for **paid cooperative office** only after layoff if an opening and combined wages cover mortgage and food.
feel: **Panicked** by expected wage loss, immediate bills and no funded replacement plan.
S2.quote: The mortgage does not pause while I find a paid route.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 thinking shock** from warehouse robots arriving around 2031.
The committee and her sister offer **pressure and leads**, not guaranteed wages.
Her concrete calls remain **reactive**, with no funded job or course arranged.

steps.text: Ask worker committee to press for paid transition time using household mortgage figures
Cancel the planned weekend trip before 2028
Ask sister about paid warehouse-office leads without assuming a vacancy
Apply for paid cooperative office vacancies after layoff only if combined wages cover mortgage and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the cooperative to show how many paid jobs it expects after 2031 and fund people to learn the warehouse office before cuts. Thinking AI reaches our code first; warehouse robots follow around 2034. I won't call the office a safe place forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more time, but my low wage and our mortgage still leave little to save. I could learn the office's delivery records if the cooperative pays me to do it. I expect my coding hours could be cut, though perhaps not all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd ask for one paid day a month with the warehouse office and enroll in its stock-control course only if the cooperative covers the fee and paid time. We'd put a small new amount from each pay cheque into emergency savings only after mortgage and food are covered. In the first year after 2031, if my coding hours fall and a paid office vacancy exists, I'd apply before giving notice and take it only if our combined wages cover the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Five years helps me learn, but I'm still expecting a loss of paid coding work. I can't study unpaid while my partner's shifts move around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the first office day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trace a returned crate from the driver's sheet to the customer's balance and ask who approves a correction. I know the software side. I need to learn the handoff before I can claim the office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the cooperative won't pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the paid office days if they are offered and keep our savings for bills. I wouldn't borrow for a certificate without a paid vacancy. A training plan written on a poster is not a pay cheque.

say: I'd demand **paid office training** and job numbers before 2031.
I'd remind colleagues **2034 robots** may later reach warehouse work.
think: I expect **coding hours** may be cut even with five years to prepare.
Our **mortgage and low wage** make unpaid study impossible.
do: Seek **paid office days** monthly and enroll in stock-control training only with employer fee and paid time.
Save a **small new payday amount** only after mortgage and food are covered.
Apply for **paid office vacancies** if coding hours fall after 2031; require combined wages covering mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of paid coding work despite more preparation time.
S3.quote: A training plan written on a poster is not a pay cheque.
fieldNote: Her five-year plan requires **paid office exposure**, not an unpaid apprenticeship.
Savings come from **new pay after essentials**, without relabeling existing cash.
The office move needs **coding cuts**, a vacancy and **bill-covering pay**.

steps.text: Enroll in stock-control course only if cooperative pays fee and work time
Save new pay after mortgage and food only when available
Apply before notice for paid office vacancies if coding hours fall and combined wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children ten years is enough to learn another skill, but I would ask the company to pay for real training now. Thinking AI reaches our code by 2036 before warehouse robots around 2039. I want workers and drivers in those plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have office experience by my early fifties if a paid place opens. The mortgage and my partner's shifting hours are problems today, with less than a month saved. A distant AI date does not make our mortgage and school bills easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer job while it pays and ask the worker committee to seek an annual paid-training report. I'd complete the cooperative's stock-control course if it funds both fee and work time; otherwise I'd use free manuals until a paid office vacancy actually requires a course I can afford beyond mortgage and food. In the first year after 2036, if coding hours end, I'd apply for paid office work where vacancies exist and keep any developer wages until a written offer covers mortgage and school costs with my partner's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Ten years gives me time to learn, but a car repair could still wipe out this month's spare money. I wouldn't plan the children's lives around a prediction that far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course worth taking at your own cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real paid office vacancy that requires it, with a fee left over after the mortgage, food and school costs. I won't take a loan to study a job that may not exist. If the money isn't there, I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about their own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn things they can explain and to ask how workers are treated. I won't choose their subjects for them. They need a secure home while they work that out.

say: I'd ask for **worker-led plans** and paid training before 2036.
I'd explain **2039 warehouse robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I might gain **paid office skills**, but no vacancy is guaranteed.
Our **thin savings** and shifting cleaning hours still make the mortgage tense today.
do: Keep **developer wages** and ask the worker committee for an annual training report.
Use **free manuals** until employer pays fee and work time, or a paid vacancy requires affordable training after mortgage, food, school.
Apply for **paid office work** after 2036 only if coding hours end and written wages cover family costs.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, despite more time before AI changes coding.
S4.quote: A distant AI date does not make our mortgage and school bills easy.
fieldNote: Her **present mortgage pressure** remains despite the decade-long scenario.
She uses **free manuals** while waiting; a course needs paid employer time or a required vacancy and affordable household bills.
She keeps any **developer wage** until a written, bill-covering office offer exists.

steps.text: Keep paid developer work while coding hours remain
Ask worker committee to request yearly paid-training reports
Use free manuals; enroll if employer pays fee/time or required vacancy leaves household essentials covered
Apply before notice if coding hours end; require written offer and combined wages covering mortgage, school

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our savings are too small for a long search and I expect the code work to go before warehouse robots reach the lifting work. Written notice, paid training, a real office vacancy and help with school costs during a gap would help us keep the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether warehouse workers can stop a bad order before a driver takes the blame. Warehouse workers lifting crates see an order mistake first. I want them beside developers when the next system is tested.

headlineQuote: Warehouse workers lifting crates see an order mistake first.
portrait: Daria is a **43-year-old experienced developer** with a bachelor's degree, maintaining food-cooperative order software.
Her **lower pay**, shifting cleaner income, two children, mortgage and under one month saved keep money tight.
She has **never used AI** and trusts warehouse records and coworkers over unproved tools.
AI Plateau already leaves her **anxious**; fast AGI overwhelms her with no funded replacement plan.
Longer timelines allow **paid office learning**, but coding cuts, real vacancies and bill-covering wages still govern a move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer wage before a paid office route is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid training, a real office vacancy and school-cost help during a gap would help.
